title: To Him we return
hook: those who, struck by loss, say we belong to Allah and to Him we return (2:156)
carry: inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un

segments.voice: Yesterday: remember Me, and your line, remembered back. Did you mention someone kindly where they couldn't hear? Today the surah keeps reading, and the next thing it promises is a test. Day three hundred forty-eight.

A phone buzzes in a family group chat: someone's uncle has died. Within minutes the replies stack up, and if the family is Muslim, many of them are the same short Arabic line, sometimes typed out in full, sometimes just the letters. Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un. Even people with little Arabic often know this line. It's said at funerals, on hearing bad news, even when a phone screen cracks. It comes from al-Baqarah, verse one hundred fifty-six. Today: to Him we return.
screen: `A MESSAGE IN THE FAMILY CHAT.` → `THE SAME SHORT LINE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` → `AL-BAQARAH, VERSE 156.`

segments.voice: Read the line where it sits. Just after remember Me comes a warning, not a comfort. God says, in the next verses, that He will surely test people with something of fear and hunger, and loss of wealth, lives and harvests. And then: give good news to the patient. Who are they? Those who, when a calamity strikes them, say, in Pickthall's words: “Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning.” Two halves. We belong to God: whatever was lost was never fully ours, and neither are we. And to Him we return: the loss isn't the end of the road. And the next verse says on such people are blessings from their Lord, and mercy, and they are the rightly guided. A hadith in Sahih Muslim shows what this did in one life. Umm Salamah heard the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ teach that whoever is struck by a loss and says these words, adding, O God, reward me in my loss and give me something better in its place, will be given something better. Then her husband, Abu Salamah, died. She said the words, and she wondered: who could be better than Abu Salamah, the first family to emigrate? She said them anyway. Later the Prophet himself asked to marry her. In the hadith, she is the one telling the story. Notice the line is spoken in the plural. We belong. We return. Even the one grieving alone says it as part of a we, which may be why it fits a family chat so well.
screen: `FIRST, A PROMISED TEST` · `WE BELONG TO GOD; WE RETURN TO HIM` · `UMM SALAMAH SAID IT ANYWAY` · `SPOKEN IN THE PLURAL`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say it when you hear of any loss. Sit, and bring to mind one loss, recent or old, large or small. Let yourself feel it for a moment, without pushing it away. Then, if you're Muslim or wish to, say the line slowly: inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un. If you don't, you can hold its two halves in English: this was never fully mine; this isn't the end of the road. Breathe with it. The bell holds the time.
To Him we return. The words of the patient in al-Baqarah, said at every loss: we belong to God, and to Him we are returning. Today's word.
Your line: inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un. Today, when you hear of any loss, yours or someone else's, let the line come to you. Day three hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: Muslims say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un on hearing of a death or any misfortune, and many add the supplication taught in Sahih Muslim asking God for reward in the loss and something better in its place.

fork.setup: you're Umm Salamah. your husband has died, and you've been taught to ask for something better in place of your loss. but who could be better than him?
options: skip the prayer; it can't be true.
fork.reveal: she said it anyway. later the Prophet asked to marry her; the hadith in Muslim is her own telling.

original.say: IN-naa lil-LAA-hi wa IN-naa i-LAY-hi raa-ji-'OON
original.note: Arabic: we belong to God, and to Him we are returning (2:156).

trapdoor: what you thought: something Muslims say when someone dies.
what it means: the answer of the patient to any loss: we belong to God, and to Him we return.
what a scholar hears: 2:155–157 frame it as the response to a promised test, and the reward is three things: blessings, mercy, and guidance.

sources.quoted: Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning.

sources.ref: Qur'an 2:155–157 (the test, the good news to the patient, blessings and mercy)
Sahih Muslim 918 (Umm Salamah and the supplication at a loss)

notes: Pickthall's 2:156 quoted as in year one; please confirm.
Sahih Muslim 918 cited from memory; the supplication ('reward me in my affliction and replace it with something better') is paraphrased. Confirm number and wording.
Abu Salamah described as from 'the first family to emigrate' (to Abyssinia, then Medina, as Umm Salamah says in the hadith); confirm phrasing.
The line is said for small losses too in common practice; the 'cracked screen' example is everyday usage, not a scholarly ruling.
The carry is Arabic transliteration exactly as the index gives it.

Pickthall 2:156 and 2:155–157 checked.
